messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Darius was nineteen, African American, single, and working as a UX designer from a small apartment that doubled as his office. He had been proud of how quickly he had found freelance work after high school, spending long hours at his laptop refining interfaces for clients he never met in person. The stalking began as something he first dismissed: repeated messages from a man he had briefly spoken with online, comments that became more personal, then persistent, then unsettlingly specific. The man seemed to know when Darius had left his building, what coffee shop he preferred, even which gym he had started using. One evening, after Darius ignored a string of messages, he found the same man waiting across the street from his apartment, staring up at the windows while pretending to scroll on his phone. Darius felt his stomach drop and hurried inside, locking the door and checking the peephole over and over until dawn.

After that night, Darius came to see ordinary life as something that could turn threatening without warning. He moved through his neighborhood with his shoulders tight, scanning cars parked near the curb, noticing faces in shop windows, and reading every unfamiliar notification as if it might be the same man again. What frightened him most was not just the possibility that the stalking could resume, but the feeling that he had already been watched for longer than he realized. He had become convinced that the world was a dangerous place, and that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. Even small routines took on a sharpened edge: walking to the corner store, leaving his studio late after a client revision, hearing footsteps on the stairwell outside his unit.

He also turned the event inward, replaying it for clues about what he had done wrong. Darius had answered the man’s first messages politely, then kept responding because he did not want to seem rude or paranoid, and later he wondered whether that had encouraged him. He blamed himself for being friendly, for not cutting things off sooner, for not trusting his discomfort from the beginning. The more he reviewed each exchange, the more certain he became that the event happened because of the way he acted. That belief made it hard for him to speak about what had happened without sounding embarrassed, and he often minimized it when friends asked why he seemed so jumpy.

Over the following weeks, Darius’s carefulness started to organize his days. He checked the lock on his apartment door several times before bed and kept the blinds partly shut while working, even in daylight. At his UX job, he found himself glancing toward the glass lobby doors whenever a notification sounded on his phone, and he began stepping away from client calls to verify who was outside his building. He stopped staying late in the shared workspace and rearranged his schedule so he could leave before dark, even when deadlines piled up. The changes protected him in the moment, but they also narrowed his life; he turned down invitations, answered fewer texts, and felt increasingly alone in the hours he spent monitoring his surroundings.

The fear did not stay abstract. It followed him into the office kitchen, down the hall to the elevator, and back home again, where he would pause at the door and listen before entering. Each new precaution seemed to confirm that something bad could happen at any time. Darius’s world grew smaller around his vigilance, and the more he tried to stay safe, the more he felt that danger was waiting just beyond whatever he could control. By the time he finally sought help, his symptoms had built to the point where work was slipping, sleep had become difficult, and he was exhausted by the constant need to watch and rethink everything he did. He came to treatment hoping to stop living as if someone were always one step behind him, but he was most afraid that if he relaxed for even a moment, he would miss the next sign and something worse would happen.
